title: Second-Order Linear Equations
lead: A second-order differential equation carries the second derivative of its unknown function. This section sorts such equations into linear and nonlinear, homogeneous and nonhomogeneous, builds general solutions from pairs of linearly independent solutions, solves equations with constant coefficients through their characteristic equation, and meets initial-value and boundary-value problems.
objectives: Recognize homogeneous and nonhomogeneous linear differential equations.
Determine the characteristic equation of a homogeneous linear equation.
Use the roots of the characteristic equation to find the solution to a homogeneous linear equation.
Solve initial-value and boundary-value problems involving linear differential equations.
summary_html:
• Second-order differential equations can be classified as linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or nonhomogeneous.
  • To find a general solution for a homogeneous second-order differential equation, we must find two linearly independent solutions. If $\kyone(x)$ and $\kytwo(x)$ are linearly independent solutions to a second-order, linear, homogeneous differential equation, then the general solution is given by $$\kyfn(x)=c_{1}\kyone(x)+c_{2}\kytwo(x).$$
  • To solve homogeneous second-order differential equations with constant coefficients, find the roots of the characteristic equation. The form of the general solution varies depending on whether the characteristic equation has distinct, real roots; a single, repeated real root; or complex conjugate roots.
  • Initial conditions or boundary conditions can then be used to find the specific solution to a differential equation that satisfies those conditions, except when there is no solution or infinitely many solutions.

exercises.prompt: Classify each of the following equations as linear or nonlinear. If the equation is linear, determine further whether it is homogeneous or nonhomogeneous. a. ${(\kydprime)}^{2}-\kyprime+8x^{3}\kyfn=0$ b. $(\sin t)\kydprime+\cos t-3t\kyprime=0$

answer.hint: Write the equation in standard form if necessary. Check for powers or functions of $\kyfn$ and its derivatives.

exercises.prompt:
Show that $\kyfn=2x^{2}$ is a solution to the differential equation

$$\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\kydprime-x\kyprime+\kyfn=0.$$

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=2x^{2},$ we have $\kyprime=4x$ and $\kydprime=4.$ Substituting into the left side, $\frac{1}{2}x^{2}(4)-x(4x)+2x^{2}=2x^{2}-4x^{2}+2x^{2}=0,$ so $\kyfn=2x^{2}$ is a solution.
answer.hint: Calculate the derivatives and substitute them into the differential equation.

exercises.prompt:
Consider the differential equation

$$\kydprime+5\kyprime+6\kyfn=0.$$

Given that $e^{-2x}$ and $e^{-3x}$ are solutions to this differential equation, show that $3e^{-2x}+6e^{-3x}$ is a solution.

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=3e^{-2x}+6e^{-3x},$ we have $\kyprime=-6e^{-2x}-18e^{-3x}$ and $\kydprime=12e^{-2x}+54e^{-3x}.$ Then $\kydprime+5\kyprime+6\kyfn=(12-30+18)e^{-2x}+(54-90+36)e^{-3x}=0,$ so $3e^{-2x}+6e^{-3x}$ is a solution, as the superposition principle predicts from the solutions $e^{-2x}$ and $e^{-3x}.$
answer.hint: Differentiate the function and substitute into the differential equation.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose the following initial-value problem models the position (in feet) of a mass in a spring-mass system at any given time. Solve the initial-value problem and graph the solution. What is the position of the mass at time $t=0.3$ sec? How fast is it moving at time $t=0.1$ sec? In what direction?

$$\kydprime+14\kyprime+49\kyfn=0,\kyfn(0)=0,\kyprime(0)=1$$

answer.solution:
$\kyfn(t)=te^{-7t}$

At time $t=0.3,$ $\kyfn(0.3)=0.3e^{(-7*0.3)}=0.3e^{-2.1}\approx 0.0367.$ The mass is 0.0367 ft below equilibrium. At time $t=0.1,$ $\kyprime(0.1)=0.3e^{-0.7}\approx 0.1490.$ The mass is moving downward at a speed of 0.1490 ft/sec.
answer.hint: Use the initial conditions to determine values for $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}.$

For each of the following problems, verify that the given function is a solution to the differential equation. Use a graphing utility to graph the particular solutions for several values of c1 and c2. What do the solutions have in common?

[T]$\kydprime+2\kyprime-3\kyfn=0;$ $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}e^{x}+c_{2}e^{-3x}$

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=c_{1}e^{x}+c_{2}e^{-3x},$ we have $\kyprime=c_{1}e^{x}-3c_{2}e^{-3x}$ and $\kydprime=c_{1}e^{x}+9c_{2}e^{-3x}.$ Then $\kydprime+2\kyprime-3\kyfn=c_{1}(1+2-3)e^{x}+c_{2}(9-6-3)e^{-3x}=0,$ so every member of the family is a solution. Graphed for several values of $c_{1}$ and $c_{2},$ the solutions all behave like $c_{2}e^{-3x}$ far to the left and like $c_{1}e^{x}$ far to the right: whenever $c_{1}\ne 0,$ the $e^{-3x}$ term dies away and the solution grows like $c_{1}e^{x}$ as $x\to\infty.$

exercises.prompt:
For each of the following problems, verify that the given function is a solution to the differential equation. Use a graphing utility to graph the particular solutions for several values of c1 and c2. What do the solutions have in common?

[T]$x^{2}\kydprime-2\kyfn-3x^{2}+1=0;$ $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}x^{2}+c_{2}x^{-1}+x^{2}\ln (x)+\frac{1}{2}$

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=c_{1}x^{2}+c_{2}x^{-1}+x^{2}\ln (x)+\frac{1}{2},$ we have $\kyprime=2c_{1}x-c_{2}x^{-2}+2x\ln (x)+x$ and $\kydprime=2c_{1}+2c_{2}x^{-3}+2\ln (x)+3.$ Then $x^{2}\kydprime=2c_{1}x^{2}+2c_{2}x^{-1}+2x^{2}\ln (x)+3x^{2}$ and $2\kyfn=2c_{1}x^{2}+2c_{2}x^{-1}+2x^{2}\ln (x)+1,$ so $x^{2}\kydprime-2\kyfn-3x^{2}+1=3x^{2}-1-3x^{2}+1=0,$ and every member is a solution. The solutions are defined for $x\gt 0;$ they all contain the part $x^{2}\ln (x)+\frac{1}{2},$ which has no arbitrary constant, so for large $x$ they all grow like $x^{2}\ln x,$ while near $0$ the term $c_{2}x^{-1}$ takes over whenever $c_{2}\ne 0.$

exercises.prompt:
For each of the following problems, verify that the given function is a solution to the differential equation. Use a graphing utility to graph the particular solutions for several values of c1 and c2. What do the solutions have in common?

[T]$\kydprime+14\kyprime+49\kyfn=0;$ $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}e^{-7x}+c_{2}xe^{-7x}$

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=c_{1}e^{-7x}+c_{2}xe^{-7x},$ we have $\kyprime=-7c_{1}e^{-7x}+c_{2}(1-7x)e^{-7x}$ and $\kydprime=49c_{1}e^{-7x}+c_{2}(49x-14)e^{-7x}.$ Then $\kydprime+14\kyprime+49\kyfn=c_{1}(49-98+49)e^{-7x}+c_{2}\big((49x-14)+14(1-7x)+49x\big)e^{-7x}=0,$ so every member is a solution. Graphed for several values of $c_{1}$ and $c_{2},$ the solutions change direction at most once and all approach $0$ as $x\to\infty,$ since $e^{-7x}$ and $xe^{-7x}$ both tend to $0.$

exercises.prompt:
For each of the following problems, verify that the given function is a solution to the differential equation. Use a graphing utility to graph the particular solutions for several values of c1 and c2. What do the solutions have in common?

[T]$6\kydprime-49\kyprime+8\kyfn=0;$ $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}e^{x/6}+c_{2}e^{8x}$

answer.solution: With $\kyfn=c_{1}e^{x/6}+c_{2}e^{8x},$ we have $\kyprime=\frac{c_{1}}{6}e^{x/6}+8c_{2}e^{8x}$ and $\kydprime=\frac{c_{1}}{36}e^{x/6}+64c_{2}e^{8x}.$ Then $6\kydprime-49\kyprime+8\kyfn=c_{1}(\frac{6}{36}-\frac{49}{6}+8)e^{x/6}+c_{2}(384-392+8)e^{8x}=c_{1}(\frac{1-49+48}{6})e^{x/6}+0=0,$ so every member is a solution. Graphed for several values of $c_{1}$ and $c_{2},$ the solutions all tend to $0$ as $x\to-\infty,$ and as $x\to\infty$ every solution with $c_{2}\ne 0$ grows like $c_{2}e^{8x}$ (positive or negative with $c_{2}$).

exercises.prompt: (Principle of superposition) Prove that if $\kyone(x)$ and $\kytwo(x)$ are solutions to a linear homogeneous differential equation, $\kydprime+p(x)\kyprime+q(x)\kyfn=0,$ then the function $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}\kyone(x)+c_{2}\kytwo(x),$ where $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ are constants, is also a solution.

answer.solution:
Let $\kyfn=c_{1}\kyone+c_{2}\kytwo.$ Differentiating term by term, $\kyprime=c_{1}\kyoneprime+c_{2}\kytwoprime$ and $\kydprime=c_{1}\kyone^{\prime\prime}+c_{2}\kytwo^{\prime\prime}.$ Substituting and collecting the terms of each solution,

$$\kydprime+p(x)\kyprime+q(x)\kyfn=c_{1}\big(\kyone^{\prime\prime}+p(x)\kyoneprime+q(x)\kyone\big)+c_{2}\big(\kytwo^{\prime\prime}+p(x)\kytwoprime+q(x)\kytwo\big)=c_{1}\cdot 0+c_{2}\cdot 0=0,$$

since $\kyone$ and $\kytwo$ are solutions. So $\kyfn=c_{1}\kyone+c_{2}\kytwo$ is also a solution.

exercises.prompt: Prove that if a, b, and c are positive constants, then all solutions to the second-order linear differential equation $a\kydprime+b\kyprime+c\kyfn=0$ approach zero as $x\to \infty \text{.}$ (Hint: Consider three cases: two distinct roots, repeated real roots, and complex conjugate roots.)

answer.solution: The roots of $a\lambda^{2}+b\lambda+c=0$ are $\lambda=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}.$ If $b^{2}-4ac\gt 0,$ the roots are distinct and real; their product $\frac{c}{a}$ is positive, so they have the same sign, and their sum $-\frac{b}{a}$ is negative, so both are negative and $c_{1}e^{\lambda_{1}x}+c_{2}e^{\lambda_{2}x}\to 0$ as $x\to\infty.$ If $b^{2}-4ac=0,$ the repeated root $\lambda=-\frac{b}{2a}$ is negative, and both $e^{\lambda x}$ and $xe^{\lambda x}$ tend to $0,$ since the exponential decays faster than $x$ grows. If $b^{2}-4ac\lt 0,$ the roots are $\alpha\pm\beta i$ with $\alpha=-\frac{b}{2a}\lt 0,$ and $|e^{\alpha x}(c_{1}\cos \beta x+c_{2}\sin \beta x)|\le e^{\alpha x}(|c_{1}|+|c_{2}|)\to 0.$ In every case all solutions approach zero as $x\to\infty.$

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

If $\kyfn$ and $z$ are both solutions to $\kydprime+2\kyprime+\kyfn=0,$ then $\kyfn+z$ is also a solution.

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

$\kyfn=e^{x}\cos (3x)+e^{x}\sin (2x)$ is a solution to the second-order differential equation $\kydprime+2\kyprime+10=0.$

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

To find the particular solution to a second-order differential equation, you need one initial condition.

answer.solution: False. The general solution of a second-order equation has two arbitrary constants, $c_{1}$ and $c_{2},$ so two conditions are needed to fix them: two initial conditions $\kyfn(t_{0})$ and $\kyprime(t_{0}),$ or two boundary conditions. One initial condition leaves a whole family; for $\kydprime+\kyfn=0$ with $\kyfn(0)=0,$ every $\kyfn=c_{2}\sin x$ satisfies it.

footnotes.html: Here and in the rest of this section the book cites Equation 17.1, the general second-order linear equation $a_{2}(x)\kydprime+a_{1}(x)\kyprime+a_{0}(x)\kyfn=\krfn(x)$; the equation substituted into and solved is $a\kydprime+b\kyprime+c\kyfn=0,$ Equation 17.2.
The book cites Example 17.1, the classification of equations; the equation meant is $a\kydprime+b\kyprime+c\kyfn=0,$ Equation 17.2.
The argument starts from functions that are linearly dependent, as the next sentence uses: there are constants $c_{1}$ and $c_{2},$ not both zero, with $c_{1}\kf_{1}(x)+c_{2}\kf_{2}(x)=0.$

Parts b, c and f give their answers as functions of $t;$ as functions of $x$ they are $\kyfn(x)=e^{-3x}(c_{1}\cos 2x+c_{2}\sin 2x),$ $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}e^{-x}+c_{2}xe^{-x}$ and $\kyfn(x)=c_{1}\cos 4x+c_{2}\sin 4x.$

With $\kyfn=c_{1}\cos 8x+c_{2}\sin 8x,$ the condition $\kyprime(0)=8c_{2}=-24$ gives $c_{2}=-3,$ so the solution of the initial-value problem is $\kyfn=3\cos 8x-3\sin 8x;$ the printed $\kyfn=3\cos(8x)$ meets $\kyfn(0)=3$ but has $\kyprime(0)=0.$
The equation is printed with $10$ for $10\kyfn;$ the answer is False for $\kydprime+2\kyprime+10\kyfn=0$ too, whose solutions are $e^{-x}(c_{1}\cos 3x+c_{2}\sin 3x).$
